title: Your fetch failed, your code wrote an empty array, and now your tests assert a lie
author: Felix Yang
summary: A scraper of mine reported that a GitHub repository had zero closed pull requests. The repository had dozens. It had its first PR closed 21 minutes after it was created , three days before the scraper ran. Nothing crashed. No test failed. The number was produced, written to disk, committed, and then quoted in a report as evidence. The bug was not that the scraper lied — it is that my pipeline had no vocabulary for "I don't know" , so it said 0 instead. The chain of custody of a wrong number Here is the whole failure, step by step. 1. A timeout that didn't look like a timeout. The fetch was a curl call with a 25-second ceiling: curl -sS --max-time 25 \ "https://api.github.com/repos/ $REPO /pulls?state=closed&per_page=100" A large repo returned ~606 KB. The body did not finish in 25 seconds, so curl killed the transfer mid-flight. curl still exited having written something to stdout, and — this is the part that matters — stdout contained the first N bytes of a perfectly valid JSON array, cut off in the middle of a string. 2. The parse error was swallowed. try : data = json . loads ( out ) except Exception : data = [] # <- the entire bug lives on this line One except Exception . It was written to be defensive and it is exactly what turned a truncation into a measurement. 3. The empty list was written to disk as a result. Downstream code received [] , counted it, and stored closed_prs: 0 . A reader of that file cannot distinguish it from a repo that genuinely has no closed PRs. The snapshot format had one slot where there should have been two. 4. The empty list was promoted to a test fixture. This is the expensive part. A regression fixture was created to cover the case "we found no evidence, so we must answer UNKNOWN ". A real repository was picked as the realistic example, and the recorded value was closed_prs: 0 — read straight from the poisoned snapshot. From that commit onward, the test suite asserted a false statement about a third party , forever, and passing tests meant the bug was invisible. 5. The only reason it was caught was that the repo was small enough to enumerate every PR with its own timestamp. On a repo with 900 PRs there would have been no way to notice, and the false fact would still be in the fixture today. Two variations of the same bug Once I started looking, the same shape showed up elsewhere in the same codebase. Variant A — a successful HTTP call that means "you are not authenticated". curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " " $API /runs" # HTTP 401 # body: {"error": {"type": "unauthorized", "message": "Invalid token"}} The check was: did curl succeed, and does the body parse as JSON? Both true. Therefore runs = [] . The dashboard reported zero runs for weeks. The token had expired on day one. An auth failure had been silently converted into a zero — and zero is a plausible number for runs, which is why nobody questioned it. Variant B — the timeout that leaves no trace at all. --max-time bounds the whole transfer. It does not bound the connect phase. Measured hang before the failure surfaced: curl -sS --max-time 30 " $URL " # ... 268,008 ms later ... # curl: (28) Operation timed out Four and a half minutes, with a 30-second timeout on the command line. If your retry logic lives above this call, your retry logic never ran. --connect-timeout is a separate, non-negotiable flag: curl -sS --connect-timeout 8 --max-time 30 " $URL " And a hung first call was enough to abort the entire scan and discard three windows of already-collected data, because one unguarded call sat outside every try . The rule: three states at every boundary The fix is not "add more error handling". It is to make EMPTY and ERROR different types that cannot be compared or coerced into each other, so that the compiler — or at least the first reader — sees the difference. I now return a small tri-state from every fetch, and nothing downstream sees a bare list: from dataclasses import dataclass OK , EMPTY , ERROR = " ok " , " empty " , " error " @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class Fetch : status : str # OK | EMPTY | ERROR items : list detail : str = "" # why it failed; never empty when status == ERROR def require ( self ): if self . status != OK : raise RuntimeError ( f " fetch { self . status } : { self . detail } " ) return self . items Four properties are doing the work here. 1. ERROR can never be downgraded. A helper that returns [] on failure is not defensive, it is a lie generator. If a caller wants to continue, it must opt in explicitly, and the failure must survive into the output. 2. EMPTY must be earned. An empty list is only a fact when the transport completed and the parser ran and the shape was checked. Anything else is ERROR : def fetch_json ( url , timeout = ( 8 , 30 )): r = subprocess . run ( [ " curl " , " -sS " , " -w " , " \n %{http_code} " , " --connect-timeout " , str ( timeout [ 0 ]), " --max-time " , str ( timeout [ 1 ]), url ], capture_output = True , text = True ) if r . returncode != 0 : return Fetch ( ERROR , [], f " curl rc= { r . returncode } : { r . stderr . strip ()[ : 200 ] } " ) body , _ , code = r . stdout . rpartition ( " \n " ) if code . strip () != " 200 " : # read the status, never infer it return Fetch ( ERROR , [], f " http { code . strip () } : { body . strip ()[ : 200 ] } " ) try : data = json . loads ( body ) except json . JSONDecodeError as e : # truncation lands here return Fetch ( ERROR , [], f " json error: { e } " ) if not isinstance ( data , list ): return Fetch ( ERROR , [], f " unexpected shape: { type ( data ). __name__ } " ) return Fetch ( OK if data else EMPTY , data ) Note what is not in that function: no bare except , and no default value that is also a legitimate result. 3. Snapshot writers must refuse to write on failure. A partial or empty write is worse than no write, because the next run diffs against it and reports fabricated change: def save_snapshot ( path , windows ): ok = [ w for w in windows if w . status == OK ] err = [ w for w in windows if w . status == ERROR ] if not ok : # nothing succeeded -> write nothing at all raise SystemExit ( 2 , f " no window fetched: { [ w . detail for w in err ] } " ) if err : # partial -> write, but name what is missing print ( f " WARNING: { len ( err ) } window(s) missing: " f " { [ w . name for w in err ] } " ) path . write_text ( json . dumps ([ w . items for w in ok ])) The rule underneath: the file on disk must never be indistinguishable from a successful run. 4. Errors must carry their own diagnosis. detail is why the failure is debuggable six weeks later without re-running anything. "fetch error: 401" is a fact; "fetch error" is a shrug. Testing the failure path without lying to yourself Two things went wrong in how this code was tested. Assert on the value that can actually be wrong. The original test asserted the number of matches found by the parser. The broken code produced the same number of matches — it was wrong about which row and what value , not about how many . Old code and new code both passed. If a test would pass with the bug present, it is not testing the bug. Assert the field that moves: assert [ p [ " closed_at " ] for p in result ] == [ " 2026-10-15T20:21:49Z " ] Use orthogonal single-point failures, not just total failure. "Everything fails" is the easy case and it exercises the least code. Run the pipeline twice: once with every fetch failing (expect: no file written, non-zero exit), and once with exactly one named window failing while the others succeed (expect: file written, missing window named, exit 0). The second run is the one that catches the swallowed exception. Never let captured data masquerade as a synthetic fixture. A fixture harvested from a live third party is a claim about the world, and the world changes. If you keep one, store the command, the timestamp, and the exit status alongside it — or replace it with a hand-written fixture and record why. A fixture that asserts a durable fact about a mutable external system is a scheduled lie. The generalisation Every one of these bugs is the same bug: a value that means "I don't know" was given the same representation as a value that means "there is nothing". It is worth hunting for on purpose, because the symptoms are quiet: A function with except Exception: return [] . A pipeline that checks if response.ok but never response.status_code . Any retry loop wrapping a call whose timeout doesn't cover connecting. Any snapshot, cache, or fixture file whose contents are valid in both the "ran and found nothing" and "never ran" cases. Any test that asserts a count. None of these raise. They all produce numbers. And a pipeline that cannot say "I don't know" will say 0 instead, which is a much more expensive answer.

title: Build a Reproducible Local Agent Tool with ArcLM (No GPU Required)
author: Ahmad Al Dibo
summary: Build a Reproducible Local Agent Tool with ArcLM (No GPU Required) An AI agent becomes useful when it can do more than generate text. It needs a way to call functions, validate their inputs, execute operations, and return structured results. But giving an agent access to tools introduces engineering questions: What arguments can a tool accept? How do you prevent an agent from running indefinitely? How can you inspect which tools were called? What happens when a tool needs permission to modify a file? How do you avoid exposing sensitive information in diagnostic output? In this tutorial, we'll build a small calculator agent with ArcLM . We'll define a typed Python function, register it as a tool, execute a bounded agent loop, inspect its trace, and examine how permissions and redaction fit into the design. No GPU or external LLM API is required. We'll use a deterministic fake model adapter so that the same example can be reproduced without API credentials or the variability of a real language model. The fake model is only a test adapter. It demonstrates the tool-calling pipeline, not the reasoning capabilities of an LLM. 1. Install ArcLM Create and activate a Python virtual environment, then install the lightweight ArcLM package: python -m venv .venv On Windows: . venv \Scripts\activate On macOS or Linux: source .venv/bin/activate Install ArcLM: python -m pip install arclm The agent runtime does not require PyTorch for this example. You don't need a GPU, a downloaded language model, or an API key. For the implementation details, see the ArcLM agent tools example . 2. Define a Typed Tool Let's start with a simple function that adds two integers. from arclm.agents import ( SideEffectLevel , ToolPermission , tool , ) @tool ( category = " utilities " , permission = ToolPermission . PURE , side_effect = SideEffectLevel . NONE , ) def add_numbers ( left : int , right : int ) -> int : """ Add two integers. """ return left + right There are only a few lines of implementation, but the metadata matters. The @tool decorator exposes the function as an ArcLM tool. Its type hints describe the expected arguments and return type, while the docstring supplies a description. The category field groups the tool with related functionality. The permission and side-effect declarations describe its operational behavior: ToolPermission.PURE identifies an operation that doesn't require access to external resources. SideEffectLevel.NONE declares that the operation has no side effects. The function itself remains ordinary Python. ArcLM supplies the tool abstraction around it. This distinction is useful when building larger systems: the business logic can remain independent of the agent runtime. 3. Register the Tool ArcLM provides ToolRegistry for managing tools by name. Create a registry and register the function: from arclm.agents import ToolRegistry registry = ToolRegistry () registry . register_tool ( add_numbers ) registered_tool = registry . get_tool ( " add_numbers " ) print ( registered_tool . name ) print ( registered_tool . description ) print ( registered_tool . input_schema ) The registry gives you a consistent way to retrieve registered tools and inspect their metadata. The input_schema describes the expected arguments. An agent adapter can use this information when deciding how to formulate a tool call. This is more explicit than simply exposing arbitrary Python functions to a model. A schema can describe what a function accepts, but it doesn't prove that a tool is safe. You still need to validate arguments and control access to operations with side effects. ArcLM's tool abstraction includes argument validation before invoking the underlying function. See src/arclm/agents/tool.py . 4. Build a Deterministic Agent A real language model would decide when to call add_numbers and what arguments to provide. That introduces an external dependency and potentially nondeterministic behavior. For this tutorial, we'll remove that variable by implementing a minimal fake model. It will do two things: Request a call to add_numbers with the arguments 2 and 5 . Read the structured tool result and return a final response. Create a file named calculator_agent.py and use the following complete example: import json from arclm.agents import ( Agent , AgentRunner , ModelResponse , SideEffectLevel , ToolCall , ToolPermission , ToolRegistry , tool , ) from arclm.security import redact_sensitive_text # 1. Define a typed tool. @tool ( category = " utilities " , permission = ToolPermission . PURE , side_effect = SideEffectLevel . NONE , ) def add_numbers ( left : int , right : int ) -> int : """ Add two integers. """ return left + right # 2. Register the tool. registry = ToolRegistry () registry . register_tool ( add_numbers ) # 3. Create a deterministic fake model adapter. class DeterministicFakeModel : def __init__ ( self ): self . calls = 0 def generate_response ( self , * , messages , tools , instructions , session , ): self . calls += 1 if self . calls == 1 : return ModelResponse ( tool_calls = [ ToolCall ( id = " call_1 " , name = " add_numbers " , arguments = { " left " : 2 , " right " : 5 , }, ) ] ) # Read the actual result returned by the tool. for message in reversed ( messages ): if message . role == " tool " : result = json . loads ( message . content ) if result [ " success " ]: return ModelResponse ( content = f " The sum is { result [ ' value ' ] } . " ) return ModelResponse ( error_code = " tool_failed " , error_message = " The calculator tool failed. " , ) return ModelResponse ( error_code = " missing_tool_result " , error_message = " No calculator result was received. " , ) # 4. Configure and run the agent. agent = Agent ( name = " calculator " , instructions = " Use the available calculator tool to add integers. " , model = DeterministicFakeModel (), tools = registry . list_tools (), ) runner = AgentRunner ( max_steps = 2 ) result = runner . run ( agent , " Add 2 and 5. " , ) if not result . success : raise RuntimeError ( f " Agent run failed: { result . error_code } " ) # 5. Inspect the result and execution trace. report = { " success " : result . success , " output " : result . output , " tool_calls " : [ call . name for call in result . session . tool_calls ], " trace_events " : [ event . event_type for event in result . trace . events ], } print ( json . dumps ( report , indent = 2 )) # 6. Demonstrate sensitive-text redaction. sample = " api_key=demo-secret " print ( redact_sensitive_text ( sample )) Run the script: python calculator_agent.py This code is intended to produce a successful calculator run followed by a redaction demonstration. Execute it with your installed ArcLM version and capture the actual terminal output before publishing the tutorial. What happens inside the agent loop? The execution follows a sequence: The runner sends the conversation and available tool descriptions to the fake model. The model returns a structured ToolCall . The runner checks whether the tool exists and is allowed. ArcLM validates the arguments and invokes the function. The tool result is added to the session. The fake model reads that result and returns a final response. Notice that the second response derives its answer from the returned tool result rather than hardcoding the number 7 . This makes the example useful for examining the interaction between an agent, a tool, and a model adapter. 5. Why Bound the Agent Loop? The line below is an important part of the implementation: runner = AgentRunner ( max_steps = 2 ) An agent that repeatedly requests tools without reaching a final response can consume resources indefinitely unless execution is constrained. max_steps limits the number of model-response steps in a run. In this example, two steps are sufficient: one tool request and one final response. The limit is not a guarantee that every run will succeed. The model could request a nonexistent tool, return an invalid response, or fail to produce a final answer. ArcLM represents execution outcomes through structured result objects, which lets the caller inspect success and failure without relying exclusively on printed text. You can explore the implementation in src/arclm/agents/runner.py . 6. Add Permission and Side-Effect Controls A calculator is a convenient first tool because it doesn't modify external state. A file-writing tool is different. It may overwrite data, create files in unintended locations, or expose information to another process. ArcLM separates permission declarations from side-effect classification. For example, a tool that writes to a local workspace could declare: from arclm.agents import ( SideEffectLevel , ToolPermission , tool , ) @tool ( category = " filesystem " , permission = ToolPermission . WRITE_LOCAL , side_effect = SideEffectLevel . REVERSIBLE , ) def write_report ( path : str , content : str ) -> str : """ Write a report to an approved workspace location. """ # Implement explicit path validation and file-writing policy here. ... This is a classification example, not a file-writing implementation. A production tool also needs to validate its destination, restrict allowed paths, handle errors, and define overwrite behavior. The distinction between the two metadata fields is important: permission declares the kind of access a tool requires. side_effect describes the operational consequences of the tool. Declaring a side effect alone does not enforce approval. ArcLM's approval policy uses the tool's permission classification and the configured ToolPolicy . By default, permissions such as WRITE_LOCAL , READ_NETWORK , EXTERNAL_ACTION , and SENSITIVE require approval. The default approval handler denies operations that require approval unless an appropriate handler is configured. For a real application, provide a ToolApprovalHandler through AgentRunner(approval_handler=...) and define how approval is requested, granted, denied, and audited. Never treat a descriptive tool schema as a substitute for access control. 7. Redact Sensitive Information Tool outputs and execution logs can contain credentials, tokens, or other sensitive values. ArcLM provides a redaction utility: from arclm.security import redact_sensitive_text sample = " api_key=demo-secret " safe_text = redact_sensitive_text ( sample ) print ( safe_text ) The intended transformation is: api_key=[REDACTED] ArcLM also redacts tool-result payloads when trace redaction is enabled by the agent's security policy. However, redaction has limits. It detects supported patterns; it cannot guarantee that every secret or item of personal information will be recognized. It is also important to distinguish tool-result redaction from complete session sanitization. For example, the session records tool-call arguments. You should not pass real credentials as tool arguments simply because result redaction is enabled. For sensitive workflows: Avoid putting secrets into prompts and tool arguments. Keep credentials in an appropriate secret-management mechanism. Minimize what you include in diagnostic output. Test redaction with representative examples from your application. The relevant implementation is available in src/arclm/security/redaction.py . 8. Inspect the Trace A final answer tells you what the agent returned. A trace helps explain how it reached that outcome. The example collects the trace event names using: trace_events = [ event . event_type for event in result . trace . events ] The runner records events such as: run_started model_responded tool_requested tool_started tool_completed step_completed run_completed These events help answer practical debugging questions. Did the model request a tool? Did the runner start it? Did it complete? Did the agent reach a final response or exhaust its step limit? For the current example, inspecting event names is enough. In a larger application, you can also examine the structured trace and result metadata. Before persisting traces, decide what information should be retained, who can access it, and how sensitive data should be handled. What This Example Demonstrates This small example separates several responsibilities that are often mixed together in agent implementations: Tools define capabilities. A typed function exposes a specific operation with a discoverable schema. The registry manages available tools. Tools can be registered and selected explicitly. The adapter defines model interaction. Our deterministic adapter demonstrates the protocol without requiring a provider. The runner controls execution. It validates tool calls, coordinates results, and limits the number of steps. Permissions and redaction address different security concerns. Permissions govern access and approval, while redaction reduces exposure of recognized sensitive values. This is not a production-ready autonomous agent, nor does it demonstrate real language-model reasoning. It is a small, inspectable foundation for understanding how tool-calling systems fit together. If you want to go further, start with the ArcLM repository and inspect the canonical custom tool agent example . The next experiment is to replace the fake adapter with a real model adapter while keeping the same tool boundary, step limit, permission policy, and trace inspection. That separation is the useful part: you can change the model backend without having to redesign the tool's Python implementation.

title: Import Incident Reconstruction: Compare Dashboard Events with a Custom Metrics API
author: MordecaiNilsson7582
summary: Short answer: choose the approach that preserves enough evidence to reconstruct why a scheduled customer-support import stopped producing results; use event analytics when operators need to explore individual runs, and use a custom metrics API when the business question and aggregation rules are stable. The dashboard is the last step, not the decision. A chart can show results_imported = 0 , yet that single number cannot distinguish an empty source, a skipped schedule, a rejected batch, or a run that never completed. For an AI support feature, those paths matter: an empty import may be valid, while a missing import can leave retrieval grounded in stale tickets. My evaluation constraint is simple: given only the retained telemetry, can an engineer explain one alert without reopening application logs or guessing? I first thought a success counter plus a failure counter would be enough. It isn't. The useful unit is an import attempt with identity, timing, outcome, and result count. Can a Business Metrics Dashboard Compare Event Analytics with a Custom API? Retain one record per scheduled attempt before deciding how to display it. At minimum, that record needs a stable run ID, schedule ID, expected time, actual start time, completion time, terminal state, result count, and a low-cardinality reason category. It should also carry the customer-support data source and deployment environment, because two simultaneous zero-result runs mean something different when they share a source than when they share only a deployment. There are two clocks. The scheduler clock answers, "Did a run begin when expected?" The production clock answers, "Did that run produce usable results before the freshness deadline?" Monitoring only completion events loses the first question. Monitoring only starts loses the second. Emit the expected schedule separately or derive it from versioned schedule configuration, then compare it with observed runs. Keep raw error text out of metric labels. Unbounded messages, ticket IDs, and run IDs create high-cardinality dimensions, which make aggregation expensive and dashboards noisy. Put those details in the per-run event or log record; expose a controlled reason such as auth , rate_limit , validation , or unknown to the aggregate layer. RFC 5424 is useful here because it separates severity from structured message content and defines ordered severity levels. A business outcome still needs its own field: a technically successful run that imports zero results isn't automatically an operational success. One alert should therefore evaluate absence and outcome together. For example: no completed run within the freshness window, or the latest completed run produced zero results when the source was expected to be nonempty. The expectation must come from business state, not a hard-coded assumption that every import always has data. That's the hinge. One Run, Four Conflicting Stories The simple approach stores one time-series point per run: timestamp, result count, and perhaps a Boolean success flag. It makes a clean line chart. It also collapses the sequence that explains an incident. If a run starts at 09:00, receives a rate-limit response, retries, and completes at 09:08 with 240 results, the final count looks healthy while the eight-minute freshness gap disappears. If only the retry error is counted, the same run looks failed. Neither projection is a faithful reconstruction. Instead, model the run as an ordered set of facts and derive dashboard metrics from it. The focused Python example below uses local data and deterministic rules, so it works in a notebook and in a production evaluator without an SDK or a vendor-specific endpoint. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime , timedelta , timezone from typing import Literal State = Literal [ " scheduled " , " started " , " completed " , " failed " ] @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class ImportEvent : run_id : str occurred_at : datetime state : State result_count : int | None = None reason : str | None = None def reconstruct ( events : list [ ImportEvent ], due_at : datetime ) -> dict [ str , object ]: ordered = sorted ( events , key = lambda event : event . occurred_at ) terminal = next ( ( event for event in reversed ( ordered ) if event . state in { " completed " , " failed " }), None , ) started = next (( event for event in ordered if event . state == " started " ), None ) return { " run_id " : ordered [ 0 ]. run_id , " started " : started is not None , " terminal_state " : terminal . state if terminal else " missing " , " result_count " : terminal . result_count if terminal else None , " late " : terminal is None or terminal . occurred_at > due_at , " reason " : terminal . reason if terminal else " no_terminal_event " , } utc = timezone . utc run = [ ImportEvent ( " run-1042 " , datetime ( 2026 , 8 , 15 , 9 , 0 , tzinfo = utc ), " scheduled " ), ImportEvent ( " run-1042 " , datetime ( 2026 , 8 , 15 , 9 , 1 , tzinfo = utc ), " started " ), ImportEvent ( " run-1042 " , datetime ( 2026 , 8 , 15 , 9 , 8 , tzinfo = utc ), " completed " , 240 ), ] summary = reconstruct ( run , due_at = datetime ( 2026 , 8 , 15 , 9 , 5 , tzinfo = utc )) assert summary [ " terminal_state " ] == " completed " assert summary [ " result_count " ] == 240 assert summary [ " late " ] is True The reducer deliberately reports a completed run as late. That distinction gives an alert evaluator a precise input without turning the dashboard into a workflow engine. It also makes replay possible: when the definition of "late" changes from five minutes to ten, recompute the projection from retained events instead of rewriting history. Now trace what a responder would see at 09:06. The schedule says run-1042 was due at 09:00, the start arrived at 09:01, and no completion has arrived, so the evaluator opens a late-run alert with no_terminal_event ; the dashboard must not call the run failed because the evidence does not yet support that claim. At 09:08 the completion event arrives with 240 results. The reducer closes the missing-terminal condition but preserves late = True , letting the incident view show both the recovered business outcome and the freshness breach. If delivery duplicates that completion at 09:09, event identity and an idempotent projection prevent another 240 results from entering the total. If events arrive out of order, their occurrence timestamps restore the run sequence while ingestion timestamps still reveal pipeline delay. One small timeline answers four questions — whether scheduling happened, whether work began, whether results became usable, and whether the telemetry itself was delayed — that a lone counter cannot answer. Retries need the same discipline. The AWS Builders' Library explains why retries are selfish and can multiply load across service layers, and why backoff with jitter helps spread repeated requests. For monitoring, record attempts under the same logical run ID and count the final business outcome once. Otherwise, a three-attempt success becomes two failures plus one success, inflating both sides of a reliability chart. 429 can be a reason category for an attempt; it should not silently become the terminal state of the logical import if a later attempt completes. Where the Evidence Lives The named tools in this question sit in different operating models. Mixpanel and Amplitude are candidates for event-oriented exploration; Metabase and Redash are candidates for querying data already available to a database or warehouse; a custom metrics API is an application-owned projection. That taxonomy is more useful than a feature checklist because incident reconstruction depends on where the durable evidence lives and who owns its schema. Approach Best fit for this import monitor Incident-reconstruction boundary Main trade-off Event analytics Operators explore run sequences, segments, and changing questions Retained events can preserve the path from schedule to result Event governance and cardinality need active control Query dashboard Run facts already land in a queryable store Reconstruction is as complete as the stored tables and joins Alert evaluation and freshness semantics may need separate ownership Custom metrics API A small, stable set of business indicators drives automation The team defines exact projections and can retain raw events elsewhere The team owns schema evolution, uptime, access control, and dashboard UX Product choice comes later. Compare Mixpanel and Amplitude by validating how each candidate retains, exports, and governs the specific run-event schema you need. Compare Metabase and Redash by testing the actual incident query against your store, including late-arriving events and access boundaries. I'm not sure a generic feature matrix can settle those questions; a replay of representative runs will. Your mileage may vary when the organization already has one of these data paths under reliable ownership. The catch is that event analytics is not suitable when the telemetry contains sensitive support content that cannot enter that system, or when operators need a tightly controlled operational endpoint rather than exploratory analysis. A custom API is not suitable when questions change weekly and the team cannot staff schema, storage, authorization, and on-call ownership. Stick with a query dashboard when the warehouse is already the timely source of truth and SQL gives responders enough detail; don't add another serving layer merely to draw the same aggregate. Make Silence Testable Treat the monitor like an eval harness. Build a compact corpus of run histories and assert the alert decision, reconstruction fields, and dashboard projection. Include an on-time nonempty completion, an on-time empty completion that is allowed by business state, a missed schedule, a started run with no terminal event, a late success, duplicate delivery, out-of-order delivery, and a retry that eventually succeeds. These are scenario classes, not invented production frequencies. Then test idempotency. Replaying the same run_id and event identity must not double the imported-result total. Test ordering by delivering completion before start. Test the boundary at exactly the freshness deadline. Finally, test configuration changes: the evaluator should retain which schedule version and threshold produced an alert, or a later responder may be unable to reproduce the decision. Prompt cost belongs in this loop if an AI component summarizes incidents. Keep alert detection deterministic; pass the reconstructed, bounded run summary to the model only after the threshold fires. Measure input tokens, output tokens, summary usefulness, and unsupported claims against the eval corpus. Don't ship raw ticket bodies merely to explain a scheduler state. A concise structured summary is easier to redact, cheaper to evaluate repeatedly, and less likely to distract the model with unrelated customer language. Sparse alerts deserve special care. A missing event cannot carry a severity level, so a separate evaluator has to notice the absence and emit an alert record. Map that record into the team's existing severity policy rather than inventing a second scale. RFC 5424 defines severity numerically from Emergency through Debug, but it does not decide whether one stale support import is critical for your business. That policy requires an explicit freshness objective and impact model. Short test suites lie. Before deployment, run the same corpus against the full path: event ingestion, storage, projection, alert evaluation, and the view responders open. A unit test of the reducer cannot reveal a delayed pipeline or a dashboard cache whose refresh interval exceeds the alert window. Roll out with shadow evaluation first, compare decisions with the current monitor, and preserve enough identifiers to explain disagreements without placing those high-cardinality IDs into aggregate labels. The Smallest Contract Worth Owning Measure reconstruction completeness before dashboard polish: the proportion of alerts for which the run, expected schedule, terminal outcome, result count, reason category, and policy version are all available. Also measure detection delay, late-event rate, duplicate-event rate, query latency during an incident, retained-event volume, and the engineering time spent changing the schema. For AI-generated summaries, add token use and evaluator-scored factual consistency. No single approach wins those dimensions. Choose event analytics when exploration and changing segmentation justify event governance. Choose a query dashboard when durable run facts already exist and the team can express the operational question safely in that data layer. Choose a custom metrics API when the contract is narrow, stable, and important enough to own. The dashboard can stay simple because the evidence underneath it isn't. References https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5424 https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/

title: How to Install ArcLM, Tokenize Text, and Run a Tiny Language Model
author: Ahmad Al Dibo
summary: How to Install ArcLM, Tokenize Text, and Run a Tiny Language Model Want to experiment with language models in Python without starting by downloading a multi-gigabyte model? You can begin with something much smaller: tokenize a sentence, create a tiny neural network, and inspect the model's output. ArcLM is a Python framework for working with language models. Its 2.0 architecture separates lightweight utilities from compute-intensive functionality, so you can install the core package without making PyTorch a mandatory dependency. In this tutorial, we'll go from installation to a model forward pass. By the end, you'll know how to: Install ArcLM without PyTorch. Convert text into token IDs. Configure and save model settings. Run a tiny native causal language model. Use the ArcLM CLI to check your installation. Prerequisites: Python 3.12, a terminal, and basic knowledge of Python. You can complete the first three steps without a GPU. 1. Install ArcLM Start by creating a virtual environment: python -m venv .venv Activate it on Windows: . venv \Scripts\activate Or activate it on macOS and Linux: source .venv/bin/activate Install ArcLM: python -m pip install arclm The core installation includes dependencies such as NumPy and SentencePiece without requiring PyTorch. Verify the installation: import arclm print ( arclm . get_version ()) For the version used in this tutorial, the output is: 2.0.0 The important point is that you can start exploring the framework without installing the runtime needed for native model execution. 2. Tokenize Your First Sentence Language models do not process ordinary text directly. They operate on numerical representations. A tokenizer converts text into tokens and maps those tokens to integer IDs. ArcLM provides a simple word tokenizer that makes this process easy to inspect: from arclm.tokenizers import Tokenizer text = " arc lm trains tiny models on local text about language models " tokenizer = Tokenizer ( max_vocab = 64 ) tokenizer . build ( text ) ids = tokenizer . encode_text ( " arc lm trains " ) print ( " Token IDs: " , ids ) print ( " Vocabulary size: " , tokenizer . get_vocab_size ()) print ( " Decoded tokens: " , tokenizer . decode ( ids )) The observed output on ArcLM 2.0.0 was: Token IDs: [2, 3, 4] Vocabulary size: 11 Decoded tokens: ['arc', 'lm', 'trains'] Here's what happens: Tokenizer(max_vocab=64) creates a tokenizer with a maximum vocabulary size of 64. build(text) constructs a vocabulary from the supplied text. encode_text() converts words into integer IDs. decode() maps those IDs back to tokens. This tokenizer is intentionally simple. It does not automatically lowercase text, so "Arc" and "arc" can be treated as different tokens. Words outside the vocabulary map to an unknown token. For more flexible subword tokenization, ArcLM also provides SentencePiece support. 3. Configure a Model Without PyTorch Configuration and execution are separate concerns. You can define settings before installing the dependency required to execute a neural network. from arclm.configs import Config config = Config ( embed_dim = 32 , block_size = 16 , num_epochs = 3 , device = " cpu " , ) print ( config . embed_dim ) print ( config . block_size ) print ( config . device ) Output: 32 16 cpu The settings describe aspects of a model or training workflow: embed_dim : the embedding dimension. block_size : the configured sequence or context length. num_epochs : the number of training epochs. device : the configured execution device. You can also save the configuration to YAML: from arclm.configs import save_config_yaml , load_config_yaml save_config_yaml ( config , " arclm-config.yaml " ) loaded_config = load_config_yaml ( " arclm-config.yaml " ) print ( loaded_config . embed_dim ) Output: 32 This allows you to keep experiment settings separate from your application code. 4. Run a Tiny Native Language Model Now let's execute a neural network. This step requires PyTorch. Install ArcLM with its training extra: python -m pip install "arclm[train]" If you need a CPU-only PyTorch installation, use the command provided by the official PyTorch installation selector . Next, create model_demo.py : import torch from arclm.tokenizers import Tokenizer from arclm.models import ArcLM text = " arc lm trains tiny models on local text about language models " tokenizer = Tokenizer ( max_vocab = 64 ) tokenizer . build ( text ) model = ArcLM ( vocab_size = tokenizer . get_vocab_size (), embed_dim = 16 , block_size = 8 , num_blocks = 1 , ) ids = tokenizer . encode_text ( " arc lm trains " )[: 8 ] input_ids = torch . tensor ([ ids ], dtype = torch . long ) logits = model ( input_ids ) print ( " Logits shape: " , tuple ( logits . shape )) print ( " Parameters: " , model . get_num_parameters ()) Run the script: python model_demo.py The observed CPU output for this configuration was: Logits shape: (1, 3, 11) Parameters: 3531 Let's break down the result. Understanding the output shape The input tensor has three dimensions of information in the processing pipeline: Batch size: 1 Sequence length: 3 Vocabulary size: 11 The input tensor itself has shape (1, 3) . The output logits have shape (1, 3, 11) . Each position in the input sequence has an associated vector of scores over the vocabulary. These scores are called logits . They are not probabilities by themselves. A generation procedure can process the logits to select a next token according to its decoding strategy. Also notice that the model contains only 3,531 parameters. It is a teaching example, not a practical replacement for a pretrained LLM. The goal is to understand the processing path: Text → Token IDs → Neural Network → Logits You have now executed a native causal language model without downloading a pretrained chat model. 5. Check the ArcLM CLI ArcLM also provides a command-line interface. To see the available commands, run: arclm --help You can alternatively use: python -m arclm --help For runtime diagnostics, run: arclm doctor The doctor command is designed to inspect the environment without requiring PyTorch. This is useful when you want to check the core installation before adding the training dependency. ArcLM's CLI includes commands for configuration, data, run inspection, caching, security, and model workflows. Commands for training, evaluation, generation, and chat require the appropriate optional dependencies. For this introduction, --help and doctor are enough. Common Issues PyTorch is missing If a model-related import raises an OptionalDependencyError , install the training extra: python -m pip install "arclm[train]" The tokenizer returns unknown tokens The words may not exist in the tokenizer's vocabulary. Build the vocabulary with more representative text, use consistent text normalization, or explore subword tokenization. The model rejects the input sequence Check the configured block_size . The sequence length must be compatible with the model's context-length configuration. The arclm command is unavailable Confirm that your virtual environment is active and that ArcLM is installed inside it. You can also use python -m arclm --help . What We Built In a few steps, we installed ArcLM, converted text into token IDs, created a configuration, and ran a tiny causal language model. We also saw why separating the lightweight core from optional compute dependencies can be useful: you can begin exploring language-model tooling before committing to a full machine-learning installation. There is an important distinction between running a randomly initialized model and using a pretrained LLM. This tutorial demonstrates the mechanics of tokenization and a forward pass, not how to build a useful conversational model. Next step: load a pretrained model and explore text generation. You can find ArcLM's source code and continue exploring the project on GitHub . If you try the examples, share your results or questions in the comments.

title: ناحیه‌های لمسی و بزرگ‌نمایی (Touch Target & Zoom): چرا اندازه و مقیاس‌پذیری در موبایل حیاتی است؟ 📱
author: Dari Tech
summary: سلام همکاران توسعه‌دهنده! 👋 امروز می‌خواهیم در مورد دو چالش بزرگ در تجربه کاربری موبایل و دسترسی‌پذیری (Accessibility) صحبت کنیم که اغلب در شلوغی توسعه فرانت‌اند نادیده گرفته می‌شوند: ناحیه‌های لمسی (Touch Targets) و بزرگ‌نمایی (Zoom) . 💡 مفهوم کلیدی دو مشکل اساسی که کاربران کم‌بینا یا کاربران موبایل با آن مواجه می‌شوند: ۱. دکمه‌ها یا لینک‌هایی که آن‌قدر کوچک یا نزدیک به هم هستند که لمس دقیق آن‌ها با انگشت دشوار یا غیرممکن است. ۲. وب‌سایت‌هایی که قابلیت بزرگ‌نمایی (Zoom) را غیرفعال کرده‌اند یا با زوم کردن، ساختار (Layout) آن‌ها به هم می‌ریزد. ⚠️ اشتباهات رایج (دام‌های طراحی) آیکون‌های شبکه‌های اجتماعی با اندازه‌ی ۱۶×۱۶ پیکسل. لینک‌های متنی چسبیده به هم بدون فاصله‌ی ایمن (مثلاً: «ویرایش | حذف»). اضافه کردن user-scalable=no یا maximum-scale=1 در متاتگ viewport . استفاده از font-size ثابت با واحد px که به تنظیمات بزرگ‌نمایی کاربر احترام نمی‌گذارد. 📏 استاندارد طلایی WCAG برای رعایت اصول دسترسی‌پذیری، این موارد را به خاطر بسپارید: حداقل اندازه ناحیه لمسی : ۲۴×۲۴ پیکسل (سطح AA در WCAG 2.2) و ترجیحاً ۴۴×۴۴ پیکسل (سطح AAA). بزرگ‌نمایی : کاربر باید بتواند تا ۲۰۰٪ زوم کند بدون اینکه محتوا بریده شود یا نیاز به اسکرول افقی پیدا کند (معیار SC 1.4.4). عدم غیرفعال‌سازی زوم : هرگز از user-scalable=no استفاده نکنید. اجازه دهید کاربر کنترل تجربه‌ی خود را در دست داشته باشد. 🛠️ راه‌حل سریع و عملی در کد ۱. ایجاد ناحیه‌ی لمسی کافی (حتی اگر آیکون کوچک است) /* ❌ اشتباه: آیکون ۱۶ پیکسلی بدون فضای ضرب‌گیر (Padding) */ .icon-btn { width : 16px ; height : 16px ; } /* ✅ درست: منطقه‌ی کلیکی ۴۴×۴۴ پیکسل، حتی اگر خود آیکون کوچک باشد */ .icon-btn { min-width : 44px ; min-height : 44px ; display : inline-flex ; align-items : center ; justify-content : center ; padding : 10px ; /* ✅ ایجاد فاصله‌ی ایمن بین دکمه‌های کناری */ } ۲. تنظیم صحیح متاتگ Viewport <!-- ❌ اشتباه: قفل کردن قابلیت زوم --> <meta name= "viewport" content= "width=device-width, initial-scale=1, maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no" /> <!-- ✅ درست: اجازه‌ی بزرگ‌نمایی کامل به کاربر --> <meta name= "viewport" content= "width=device-width, initial-scale=1" /> ۳. رعایت فاصله بین لینک‌ها یا دکمه‌های کناری (با React و Tailwind) // ❌ اشتباه: لینک‌ها بدون فاصله و چسبیده به هم < a href = "/edit" > ویرایش </ a > < a href = "/delete" > حذف </ a > // ✅ درست: استفاده از دکمه‌های مجزا با فاصله‌ی استاندارد و ارتفاع کافی < div className = "flex gap-4" > < button className = "min-h-[44px] px-4" > ویرایش </ button > < button className = "min-h-[44px] px-4" > حذف </ button > </ div > ۴. استفاده از واحدهای اندازه‌گیری نسبی /* ❌ اشتباه: فونت با واحد px ثابت که به تنظیمات کاربر واکنش نشان نمی‌دهد */ .title { font-size : 16px ; } /* ✅ درست: استفاده از rem که به تنظیمات پیش‌فرض مرورگر کاربر احترام می‌گذارد */ .title { font-size : 1.25rem ; } 🔗 ابزارهای پیشنهادی برای تست برای اطمینان از کیفیت کد خود، از این ابزارها استفاده کنید: Chrome DevTools : بخش Rendering → فعال کردن CSS overview (برای بررسی بصری اندازه‌ها و کنتراست). Lighthouse : بخش Accessibility → بررسی هشدار “Touch targets are sized appropriately”. تست دستی : هیچ‌چیز جای تست روی یک دستگاه موبایل واقعی را نمی‌گیرد! 👁️ قانون ۳ ثانیه‌ای : سایت را روی موبایل باز کنید و با انگشت شست روی یک دکمه‌ی کوچک ضربه بزنید. اگر ۲ بار از ۳ بار اشتباه زدید (یا لمس شما روی دکمه‌ی کناری ثبت شد)، ناحیه‌ی لمسی (Touch Target) مشکل دارد. سپس ۳ بار زوم کنید (با پینچ روی موبایل یا Ctrl + در دسکتاپ)؛ اگر ساختار صفحه شکست یا به هم ریخت، یعنی مشکل بزرگ‌نمایی (Zoom) دارید. 🗣️ نوبت شماست! شما چطور اطمینان حاصل می‌کنید که رابط کاربری‌تان برای همه‌ی کاربران (از جمله کاربران موبایل و کم‌بینا) قابل استفاده است؟ آیا ابزار یا ترفند خاصی برای تست دسترسی‌پذیری در گردش کار (Workflow) خود دارید؟ تجربه‌ها و نظرات خود را در بخش کامنت‌ها با من و سایر توسعه‌دهندگان به اشتراک بگذارید! 👇💬

title: Firefox Enterprise Is Here. How to Get Its AI Controls Free with policies.json
author: Alan West
summary: If you run plain Firefox, at home or on a fleet of laptops managed with a policies.json file, Firefox Enterprise takes nothing away from you. Mozilla is charging for a self-hosted management console and the security features built around it. The browser stays free, and the AI lockdown Mozilla lists as an enterprise feature already works today through the free AIControls policy in policies.json . What Mozilla won't tell anyone yet is the price, which is a strange choice when Google prints $6 per user per month on its own product page and gives its basic console away for $0. Mozilla announced Firefox Enterprise on October 12, 2026 . I went through the announcement, the two product pages, Mozilla's policy docs and the Lobsters thread where people are already fighting about it. Below is what the paid product adds, what the free browser keeps, and how it compares with Chrome Enterprise and Edge for Business. What Firefox Enterprise actually is The announcement covers the Firefox browser, the Gecko engine it's built on, and a management console "organizations can run on their own infrastructure." The Firefox Enterprise landing page lists what that console gets you: centralized policy control across endpoints controls over the browser's outbound connections and telemetry native DLP to "warn or block sensitive data actions by domain" AI controls to "allow, restrict or disable AI tools" SIEM integration to "export browser events and audit activity" a Lockdown Mode for high-risk or restricted browsing extension governance across the whole org Professional Support, described as "private triage and defined response times" The product detail page adds device-posture gating, corporate SSO integration, and a way for content analysis tools you already run, like Trellix and Broadcom, to extend into the browser. It also claims tiered access for managed and unmanaged devices "without MDM, VPN or EDR". Sales start in France, Germany, Austria and Switzerland, with more markets to follow. Thunderbird Enterprise is in development. There's no public price for either: the product page says "a subscription model" and the only call to action is a "Request a Demo" form. What stays free for regular Firefox users Nothing in the announcement or on the product pages says anything changes for the roughly 200 million people who use Firefox every month. The free enterprise tooling Firefox has had for years is still documented and shipping: enterprise policies through Group Policy ADMX templates, Intune OMA-URI, macOS configuration profiles, or a plain policies.json file Firefox ESR for orgs that want a slower update cadence free public support: docs, the knowledge base and community forums The policy engine is the part to watch. Whatever the console does to the browser presumably ends up as policy on the client, and today that client side is open, documented and free, with AI controls already built in. Block Firefox AI features with policies.json, for free If AI governance is what's pushing your security team toward a paid product, look at what the free policies already cover. The AIControls reference lists keys for Default , Translations , PDFAltText , SmartTabGroups , LinkPreviewKeyPoints , SidebarChatbot , SmartWindow and SpeechRecognition . Each takes a Value ( "available" or "blocked" ) and a Locked boolean. Blocking an on-device feature also deletes the models it already downloaded. It needs Firefox 149.0.2 or later. On Linux, put this in /etc/firefox/policies/policies.json : { "policies" : { "DisableTelemetry" : true , "AIControls" : { "Default" : { "Value" : "blocked" , "Locked" : true } } } } On Windows, the file goes in a distribution folder next to firefox.exe . On macOS it goes in Firefox.app/Contents/Resources/distribution . Restart Firefox, then open about:policies to check that it loaded. One gotcha: the old policy-templates page now opens with a warning that it is "NOT current". Policy behavior and syntax have moved to the Firefox administrator reference . Read the entry there before you lock anything fleet-wide. That covers the policy part of Firefox Enterprise for $0. What the free route doesn't give you is a central console, reporting, DLP, SIEM export or someone at Mozilla to call. Firefox Enterprise vs Chrome Enterprise vs Edge for Business Mozilla looks weakest here, and not only on price. Firefox (free) Firefox Enterprise Chrome Enterprise Core Chrome Enterprise Premium Edge for Business Price $0 Not published $0 $6/user/month Management service built into the Microsoft 365 admin center, no separate price listed Policy delivery GPO, Intune, profiles, policies.json Self-hosted console Cloud, Google Admin console Cloud, Google Admin console Cloud, Microsoft 365 admin center Where management runs Your own tooling Your servers Google's cloud Google's cloud Microsoft's cloud DLP No Yes No Yes Not in the management service Vendor support Community, or paid upgrade Included Separate support plan Not stated on the product page Microsoft Support Engine Gecko Gecko Chromium Chromium Chromium Google gives away the kind of console Mozilla is charging for. Chrome Enterprise Core lets you set policies, force-install and pin extensions, and get version reporting from the cloud for nothing. Google only charges for DLP and zero-trust access, in Premium. Microsoft's Edge management service sits inside the Microsoft 365 admin center with no separate price listed, and covers policies, extensions and AI features. Mozilla can't win on features per dollar, so the pitch is about where things run: the console sits on your hardware, its data stays inside your boundary, and the engine isn't Chromium. CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo puts it as "If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, 'choice' is a lie." For a German ministry working through NIS2 and DORA, both of which Mozilla lists on the enterprise page, that argument beats any feature checklist. For a 40-person startup on Google Workspace it's irrelevant. Paid support, and where it could go wrong The enterprise page says standard support "is included with Firefox Enterprise, and is available as a paid upgrade if you're using Firefox as your company's browser." That part isn't new. Heise reported in November 2025 on "Firefox Support for Organizations", which started in January 2026 with a private ticket channel, defined response times and discounted custom feature work, and Mozilla said then that public support would stay free. I have no problem with a paid support desk. I'd have a problem if fixes for paying customers started landing faster than fixes for everyone else. Mozilla hasn't said that will happen and I've seen no evidence it will, but Mozilla has asked people to take things on trust before. Why the skeptics showed up The Lobsters thread splits about how you'd expect. One commenter says their job "outlawed Firefox and made Chrome our exclusive browser precisely because Firefox didn't have an Enterprise offering," which is about the best case for this product existing. The top comment says Mozilla "need[s] a non-Google revenue stream", and that's fair: It's FOSS notes Mozilla "still depends on Google through its search partnerships", and enterprise sales won't replace that money soon. The other side is about leadership: the CEO pay complaint, the IoT and AR/VR detours, and a pointed observation that Mozilla is a US company selling sovereignty to Europe. A Mozilla engineer in the thread says "most of the code is open source", which prompted the obvious follow-up about releasing the rest. It's FOSS makes the same point: "Self-hosted doesn't automatically mean open source." Nobody has confirmed whether the console source will be published. If Mozilla wants the Lobsters crowd on side, that's the cheapest win available. My take: I'd rather Mozilla make money from IT departments than from ad tech experiments. The structure looks right, with the browser and policy engine free and a paid console and SLA for orgs that need one. What bothers me is how opaque it all is: there's no pricing, no console source, and no written promise that the free policy engine stays complete. If Mozilla published those, I think most of the suspicion would go away. Checklist if you manage Firefox today Do nothing urgent. Your policies.json , ADMX templates and ESR channel keep working. Read the AIControls entry and decide your default before your security team asks. Check about:policies on a sample machine to confirm what's actually applied. If you're in the DACH region or France and need DLP or SIEM export without a US cloud console, request a demo and get a real per-seat number to hold up against Chrome Premium's $6. The same Mozilla engineer replied to the "we got banned" story with: "Would be cool if they told us what's missing." So I'll ask here. If your company dropped Firefox for Chrome or Edge, what was the actual blocker, and would a self-hosted console with no public price change that decision? title: I built a free tool that turns AI-generated Markdown tables into Excel

title: I built free PDF tools that never upload your files
author: PDF Utils
summary: A while ago I needed to merge two PDFs. Every "free online PDF tool" I found worked the same way: upload your file to someone's server, wait, download the result. A bank statement, a contract, a medical form - straight to a machine I know nothing about, running code I can't see, under a privacy policy I'll never read. That bothered me enough to build an alternative: PDF Utils ( https://yourpdfutils.com/ ), a set of PDF tools that run entirely in your browser. The file never leaves your device. Not "encrypted in transit", not "deleted after an hour" - it simply never goes anywhere. What "runs in your browser" actually means Merging, splitting, compressing, rotating, extracting pages, converting images, signing - all of it happens in JavaScript on your machine. When you drop a file on the page, it's read locally, processed locally, and saved back to your downloads. Once a tool page is loaded, nothing about your file is sent anywhere. There's no account system because there's nothing an account would be for. No upload queues, no "your file will be ready shortly". The only real limit is your device's own memory. The parts that were harder than they look Performance. Moving processing to the client means the user's phone is now the server farm. Long operations need honest progress reporting or people assume the tab crashed, and heavy work has to yield to the UI thread or the page freezes. I spent more time on "feels instant" than on the PDF logic itself. 45 languages. The interface ships in 45 languages. Short tool labels are the hardest kind of text to translate well: a word like "Sign" can mean a signature or a street sign, RTL languages need real layout testing, and plural rules differ wildly. I'd rather grow the list slowly with review than ship 45 machine-translated interfaces. Compression honesty. "Compress PDF" tools love to promise 90% reductions. A PDF of scanned pages compresses very differently from one born digital, so no honest tool can promise a fixed number. The tool does what the file allows and shows you the real result. The business model It's free, supported by ordinary ads instead of subscriptions, watermarks, or "3 tasks per day" limits. Ads align incentives the right way for a tool like this: the site earns when people use the tools, not when they hand over data or a credit card. There's nothing to cancel because you never signed up for anything. What's next More tools, more languages, faster processing. If there's a PDF task you still open a desktop app for, I'd like to hear what it is. https://yourpdfutils.com/

title: Mercor: solo 208 de 923 ocupaciones con cobertura real de IA
author: lu1tr0n
summary: Un chatbot resuelve casi cualquier pregunta de programación en segundos, pero nadie sabe si uno hace bien el trabajo real de un electricista, una enfermera o un inspector de seguridad. Según un informe de Mercor , apenas 208 de las 923 ocupaciones de EE.UU. tienen una tarea medida por benchmarks de IA con cinco pruebas o más. La cifra agregada es más contundente: el 90% de las horas de trabajo pagadas en el país caen en tareas que las pruebas de IA actuales apenas rozan. TL;DR Mercor halla que solo 208 de 923 ocupaciones de EE.UU. tienen benchmarks de IA con 5 o más tareas cubiertas.- El 90% de las horas laborales del país caen en tareas con poca o nula cobertura de pruebas de IA.- Veintinueve benchmarks mapean 18.797 tareas O*NET agrupadas en 22 familias laborales, según el estudio.- Seis de 22 familias de empleo, entre ellas salud y educación, no tienen ninguna ocupación bien cubierta.- La cobertura sigue el salario: Computación y Matemáticas llega a 29 de 36 ocupaciones medidas. Qué es el Benchmark Map de Mercor El Benchmark Map de Mercor es un índice público que cruza las 923 ocupaciones y las 18.797 tareas de la taxonomía O*NET del Departamento de Trabajo de EE.UU. con 29 benchmarks de IA existentes, para medir qué porción del trabajo real del país tiene al menos una prueba que lo evalúe. Mercor es conocida en la industria por operar un marketplace que conecta expertos de distintas profesiones con laboratorios de inteligencia artificial para generar datos de entrenamiento y evaluación. Su propio benchmark, APEX, forma parte de los 29 incluidos en este índice, con la ventaja de que la empresa tiene acceso a prompts aún no publicados y puede mapearlos directamente a cada tarea O*NET. Qué pasó El informe, publicado por Mercor y disponible como mapa interactivo, cruza la taxonomía O*NET con 29 benchmarks de evaluación de modelos de IA. Según el estudio , de las 923 ocupaciones que componen la fuerza laboral estadounidense, solo 208 tienen al menos una tarea con cinco o más prompts de algún benchmark mapeados a ella. La cifra agregada confirma el problema: nueve de cada diez horas de trabajo pagadas en el país corresponden a tareas sin ningún benchmark o con una cobertura mínima, según el mismo informe. Mercor agrupó las 923 ocupaciones en 22 familias laborales siguiendo la clasificación oficial de O*NET, y encontró que 6 de esas 22 familias, que incluyen salud y educación, no tienen una sola ocupación con cobertura real. El mapa divide esas 923 ocupaciones en 22 familias que siguen la clasificación estándar de O*NET, desde Computación y Matemáticas hasta Práctica de la Salud. Cada ocupación aparece como una celda que se colorea según el porcentaje de sus tareas con cobertura, lo que permite ver de un vistazo qué sectores concentran casi toda la atención de las pruebas de IA actuales y cuáles quedan prácticamente a oscuras. El informe cubre 18.797 tareas repartidas en 923 ocupaciones de EE.UU. Contexto e historia Los benchmarks que miden qué tan bien razona o programa un modelo se multiplicaron en los últimos años, pero casi todos nacieron para medir capacidades académicas o de ingeniería de software, no el trabajo que sostiene el resto de la economía. Mercor dice que este Benchmark Map es apenas su primer paso hacia un recurso que planea actualizar de forma continua. La idea de medir qué tan expuesta está una ocupación a la IA no es nueva. En 2023, los investigadores Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin y Daniel Rock publicaron un estudio que etiquetó miles de tareas de O*NET según cuánto podía acelerarlas un modelo de lenguaje. Mercor retoma esas etiquetas binarias de exposición y las cruza con su propio mapa de cobertura para ver si las pruebas de IA realmente se concentran donde la exposición es mayor. El propio informe reconoce que la saturación de pruebas de IA en ingeniería de software no es casual: ese es el tipo de tarea donde es más fácil automatizar la evaluación, porque hay tests, métricas de éxito claras y repositorios públicos, y donde los laboratorios de IA tienen interés directo en medir el progreso de sus propios modelos. Por eso Mercor impuso un tope de benchmarks por familia laboral al armar su índice de 29 pruebas, para que ingeniería de software y investigación académica no dominaran el panorama como lo hacen en catálogos previos. Cómo mide Mercor los benchmarks de IA El mecanismo detrás del mapa es un juez automático. Mercor usa un modelo de lenguaje para leer cada prompt de los 29 benchmarks evaluados y asignarle una o varias tareas de la lista de 18.797 que define O*NET; un mismo prompt puede mapear a varias tareas distintas si evalúa habilidades que se superponen. Una tarea O*NET cuenta como cubierta únicamente si el juez le asignó cinco o más prompts entre todos los benchmarks, no basta con una mención aislada. Para confirmar que el etiquetado automático no inventaba coincidencias, el equipo comparó las etiquetas del juez con las de expertos humanos sobre APEX, el propio banco de pruebas de Mercor, donde la empresa tiene acceso a prompts todavía no publicados. Esa validación es la que permite afirmar que la cobertura medida no es ruido estadístico, sino una aproximación razonable a qué mide cada prueba. Los 29 benchmarks del índice se eligieron con cinco criterios: Disponibilidad pública : al menos 25 tareas públicas, o acceso directo vía APEX en el caso de Mercor.- Tareas agénticas : pedirle al modelo que ejecute una tarea, no solo que responda preguntas sobre ella.- Realismo económico : tareas parecidas a las que una empresa real le pide a un empleado, no acertijos académicos.- Diversidad económica : un tope de benchmarks por familia laboral para que software e investigación no dominen el índice.- Dificultad balanceada : benchmarks que los modelos de frontera todavía no saturan. Para entender por qué unas ocupaciones tienen más cobertura que otras, Mercor corrió una regresión logística a nivel de tarea: la probabilidad de cobertura se explica con la etiqueta de exposición a la IA de Eloundou et al. y el logaritmo de la masa salarial de la ocupación, calculada multiplicando el salario medio que reporta la Oficina de Estadísticas Laborales por la cantidad de trabajadores y una semana de 40 horas. Los errores estándar se agrupan por familia ocupacional y los intervalos de confianza del 95% usan el método delta. El resultado de esa regresión es una curva, no una tabla simple: a medida que sube la masa salarial de una ocupación, la probabilidad estimada de que una de sus tareas esté cubierta por algún benchmark sube de manera consistente, y la brecha entre tareas de alta y baja exposición a la IA se mantiene casi constante en todo el rango salarial. Ser una tarea automatizable según Eloundou et al. ayuda, pero ayuda mucho menos que pertenecer a una ocupación bien pagada. flowchart TD A [ "Taxonomia O*NET: 923 ocupaciones, 18797 tareas" ] -- > B [ "Juez LLM etiqueta cada prompt de benchmark con sus tareas O*NET" ] B -- > C [ "Validacion contra etiquetas humanas en APEX" ] C -- > D { "Tarea con 5 o mas prompts mapeados?" } D -- >| "Si" | E [ "Tarea cubierta" ] D -- >| "No" | F [ "Tarea sin cobertura" ] Impacto y análisis Solo 29 benchmarks conforman el índice inicial del Benchmark Map. El hallazgo más incómodo del informe es el patrón detrás del número total de ocupaciones cubiertas, más que el número en sí. Los benchmarks de IA no se reparten al azar entre las 923 ocupaciones: la probabilidad de que una tarea tenga cobertura sube con la masa salarial de la ocupación a la que pertenece, y sube todavía más si esa tarea ya está etiquetada como expuesta a la IA. El ejemplo que da Mercor es contundente: las tareas de abogados, una ocupación de alta exposición y alto salario, están ampliamente cubiertas, pero tareas igual de expuestas en ocupaciones como secretarias legales o empleados de juzgados apenas aparecen en algún benchmark. Familia laboral (O*NET)Ocupaciones cubiertasCoberturaComputación y Matemáticas29 de 3680,6%Servicio comunitario10 de 1471,4%Legal5 de 771,4%Negocios y Finanzas33 de 4868,8%Administración y oficina21 de 5141,2%Gerencia21 de 5637,5%Arquitectura e Ingeniería19 de 5633,9%Artes y Medios13 de 4032,5%Ventas6 de 2227,3%Ciencia15 de 6025,0%Educación y Bibliotecas9 de 6214,5%Práctica de la Salud12 de 8913,5% La tabla muestra solo 12 de las 22 familias para no diluir el patrón, pero la tendencia se mantiene en el resto: cuanto más grande es la nómina agregada de una familia laboral, más probable es que algún benchmark la mida, incluso cuando ocupaciones de menor salario comparten el mismo nivel de exposición a la IA según la clasificación de Eloundou et al. El informe llama a esto la larga cola del trabajo de ingresos medios: ocupaciones como asistentes administrativos, técnicos de laboratorio o coordinadores de proyectos rara vez aparecen en un paper de benchmarks, aunque sumen millones de horas trabajadas al año. Sin una medición directa de esas tareas, cualquier afirmación sobre qué tan buena es la IA en el trabajo real descansa sobre una muestra sesgada hacia el código y las finanzas. 💭 Clave: la exposición a la IA de una tarea importa menos que el salario de la ocupación a la hora de decidir si alguien se molestó en medirla. Qué sigue Mercor dice que este mapa es un recurso vivo, no un informe cerrado: planea sumar más pruebas al índice a medida que aparezcan benchmarks con mayor realismo económico, y ampliar la cobertura hacia las familias laborales que hoy quedan en cero, como salud y educación. El objetivo declarado es que cualquiera pueda consultar, ocupación por ocupación, qué tan bien evaluada está la IA frente al trabajo que esa persona hace todos los días. 📖 Resumen en Telegram: Ver resumen Si evaluás modelos de IA o diseñás benchmarks, abrí el mapa interactivo de Mercor y filtrá la familia laboral de tu propia industria para ver cuántas de sus tareas tienen alguna prueba real detrás. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Qué mide exactamente el Benchmark Map de Mercor? Mide qué porción de las 18.797 tareas que O*NET usa para describir el trabajo en Estados Unidos tiene al menos una prueba de modelos de IA que la cubra con cinco o más prompts, agrupando el resultado por las 923 ocupaciones y 22 familias laborales del país. ¿Cuántas de las 923 ocupaciones de EE.UU. están bien cubiertas? Solo 208 tienen una tarea con cinco o más prompts mapeados por el índice de Mercor; el resto, unas 715 ocupaciones, no alcanza ese umbral o no tiene ninguna prueba asociada. ¿Por qué las ocupaciones legales están mejor evaluadas que las administrativas? Porque la cobertura del Benchmark Map sigue más de cerca la masa salarial de la ocupación que su exposición real a la IA: abogados, con salarios altos, están bien cubiertos, mientras secretarias legales y empleados de juzgados, con exposición similar según Eloundou et al., quedan casi sin pruebas. ¿Qué es la exposición a la IA de Eloundou et al.? Es una etiqueta binaria que ese estudio de 2023 asignó a miles de tareas de O*NET según cuánto podía acelerarlas un modelo de lenguaje grande; Mercor la usa como variable de control para separar el efecto del salario del efecto de la exposición real. ¿Mercor seguirá actualizando este índice de benchmarks? Sí: la empresa lo describe como un primer paso hacia un recurso que planea actualizar de forma continua, sumando benchmarks y ocupaciones conforme aparezcan pruebas con suficiente realismo económico. Referencias Mercor Benchmark Map : el informe original con el mapa interactivo de cobertura por ocupación.- O*NET Resource Center : la taxonomía oficial del Departamento de Trabajo de EE.UU. con las 923 ocupaciones y sus tareas.- Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin y Rock (2023) : el estudio que etiquetó la exposición de cada tarea de O*NET a los modelos de lenguaje.- Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics: la fuente de los salarios usados para calcular la masa salarial de cada ocupación. 📱 ¿Te gusta este contenido?
